cues.text: An Englishman's Missionary Vocation
Born around 675 near Crediton in the English kingdom of Wessex and originally named Winfrid , Boniface entered monastic life as a boy.

He rose within the English Benedictine world to a position of real comfort and respect, skilled enough as a teacher and writer that he might easily have spent his whole life advancing quietly within his own community.
Instead, drawn by a missionary vocation that had already sent other English monks across the Channel to evangelize the still-pagan Germanic peoples, Winfrid abandoned this secure path entirely.

He made a first, unsuccessful missionary attempt to Frisia in 716 before traveling to Rome, where Pope Gregory II renamed him Boniface and commissioned him as a missionary bishop for the vast, largely unorganized territory of Germania.
An Axe Against a God of Thunder
The most celebrated episode of Boniface's long missionary career took place at Geismar in Hesse.
Local pagans venerated a massive oak sacred to Donar , the Germanic god of thunder—a tree believed to strike down with divine vengeance anyone who dared threaten it.
Before a crowd fully expecting to witness his destruction, Boniface deliberately took an axe to the sacred oak, felling it as onlookers watched in tense expectation of the thunder-god's wrath.
When no lightning fell and no vengeance came, the visible, public collapse of the old gods' supposed power convinced large numbers of witnesses to embrace baptism on the spot.
Boniface used the felled tree's own timber to build a Christian chapel on the very site of the pagan shrine.
Founder and Reformer
Across three decades of tireless labor, Boniface organized new dioceses throughout the German territories and consecrated bishops.
He founded numerous monasteries to anchor and sustain the young Christian communities he established, among them the great abbey of Fulda .
It would become one of the most important centers of learning in the whole of medieval Europe.
Beyond evangelizing pagan territory, Boniface also undertook the difficult work of reforming the Frankish clergy.
Their discipline and moral standards had grown seriously lax in the political chaos of the preceding century.
He worked closely with the papacy and rising Carolingian rulers to bring Frankish Church practice into closer alignment with Roman order and discipline.
A Final Mission at an Advanced Age
Even as an old man, honored and secure in the authority his decades of labor had earned him, Boniface refused to settle into comfortable retirement.
In 754, well into his seventies, he set out on one final missionary journey into Frisia .
It was the very region where his first missionary attempt, decades earlier, had ended in failure.
He was determined, it seems, to close his life exactly where his vocation had first begun.
Martyred with the Gospel in His Hands
On June 5, 754, while gathered with a group of recent converts awaiting confirmation near Dokkum, Boniface's party was attacked by a band of hostile pagans.
Tradition holds that Boniface forbade his companions to take up arms in his defense and was killed, together with dozens of his companions.
He was still holding a Gospel book he had raised, by some accounts, to shield himself from the fatal blow—a book later recovered bearing the marks of the attack.
It has been preserved ever since as one of the most treasured relics associated with his martyrdom.
Legacy
Boniface's relics were carried to Fulda, the monastery he himself had founded, where they remain venerated to this day as the spiritual heart of German Catholicism.
Honored as the Apostle of Germany and patron of the German-speaking lands, Boniface remains a model of missionary courage sustained across an entire lifetime.

He twice left safety behind to answer the same difficult call and died, in the end, exactly as he had lived for thirty years: unarmed, undeterred, and holding fast to the Gospel he had crossed a continent to proclaim.
